extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and writers studying or producing work in the Négritude/postcolonial francophone literary tradition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative dimensions for literary, poetic, and visual works aligned with the Négritude movement: their political aims, thematic concerns, stylistic features, and cultural strategies. Useful for authors or critics assessing whether a work embodies Négritude's principles and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to colonialism and denunciation of European domination
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement was characterized generally by opposition to colonialism, denunciation of Europe's alleged inhumanity, and rejection of Western domination and ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive Négritude texts explicitly critique colonial structures and European claims of cultural superiority. Works should foreground anti-colonial argument or portrayals of colonial injustice rather than assimilative or apologetic stances. Examples: Césaire's denunciations of assimilation and of Western imperialism as causing an 'inferiority complex.' Anti-pattern: neutral or celebratory depictions of colonial systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise and cultivate black consciousness (reimagining 'blackness')
rubrics_metrics.description: Aimed at raising and cultivating 'black consciousness' across Africa and its diaspora; re-imagining the derogatory term 'nègre' as an emic form of empowerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective works promote awareness, pride, and collective self-understanding among Black readers and communities. They may reclaim formerly pejorative language and transform it into positive identity markers. Example: Césaire's deliberate incorporation of 'nègre' into Négritude as empowerment. Scoring note: stronger works make black consciousness an explicit thematic or rhetorical focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decolonization of the mind / psychological emancipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on acceptance and pride in being black as a means by which the 'decolonization of the mind' can be achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Texts should attempt to dismantle internalized inferiority (the psychological effects of colonialism) and foster self-valuation. Césaire frames acceptance of blackness as countering Western-imposed inferiority. Anti-pattern: works that reinforce colonial stereotypes or prioritize external validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrealist-informed literary style
rubrics_metrics.description: The writers drew heavily on a surrealist literary style and were sometimes influenced by Surrealist stylistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal features to look for include surreal imagery, dreamlike associations, juxtaposition of unexpected elements, and non-linear or symbolic poetics. Many founding Négritude poets used surrealist technique to convey subjectivity and rupture with colonial discourse. Scoring: authenticity is higher when surrealist devices are used to serve anti-colonial/identity aims rather than as mere ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with Marxist and black radical political philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectuals employed Marxist political philosophy, in the black radical tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works often situate racial oppression within class or global capitalist critiques; they may highlight economic exploitation, class inequalities, and calls for structural change. Inclusion of Marxist analysis or solidarity with anti-capitalist themes strengthens alignment with this strand of Négritude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploration of diasporic being, identity, and belonging
rubrics_metrics.description: Often explored the experience of diasporic being, asserting one's self and identity, and ideas of home, home-going and belonging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives and poems should interrogate displacement, double-consciousness, and the experience of living between cultures. Effective works treat belonging/return/home-going as complex processes rather than simple nostalgia. Influence from Harlem Renaissance and transatlantic dialogue is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and celebration of African history, traditions, and culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of and pride in being black and a celebration of African history, traditions, and beliefs; promotion of African culture into Western modernity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art and literature should valorize African cultural forms, histories, and practices, integrating them into modern artistic expression. This can include myth, oral traditions, vernacular idioms, or visual motifs. Anti-pattern: erasure or denigration of African cultural sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of neologism and rhetorical re-signification (e.g., 'Négritude')
rubrics_metrics.description: The movement's name itself is a constructed noun from 'nègre' + '-itude' used to trope and re-signify racist vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic linguistic moves—coinage, reappropriation, and redefinition of derogatory terms—are hallmark devices. Works that consciously reframe racist language and scientific racism vocabularies (as Césaire did) align with movement tactics. Caution: such re-signification should be deliberate and contextualized, not casual reuse of slurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militant cultural and political stance (Damas' approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A militant style of defending 'black qualities' and rejection of reconciliation with Caucasians; focus on concrete social and political themes like poverty, illiteracy, exploitation, forced labor and social racism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some Négritude works are explicitly polemical and confrontational, listing injustices and calling for awareness or action. Damas' anthology explicitly frames indigenous poetry around themes of exploitation, inequality and resistance. Works should not shy away from naming structural abuses if aligned with this strand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different strategic orientations within movement (e.g., Senghor's universal valuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variations existed: Senghor advocated modern incorporation of traditional African customs and sought a 'seat at the [French] table as equals' rather than separate political radicalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work follows a more assimilationist/conciliation strategy (valuing African culture within broader civic frameworks) or a separatist/militant one. Both are historically part of Négritude; evaluation should note which orientation the work represents and how coherently it carries that approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intertextual dialogues with Harlem Renaissance and diaspora intellectuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Négritude was influenced by the Harlem Renaissance and writers such as Langston Hughes, Claude McKay, and W. E. B. Du Bois; the Nardal sisters acted as conduits for these exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger Négritude-aligned works often engage with African American/Caribbean diasporic texts, themes, and forms—acknowledging cross-Atlantic intellectual exchange. Presence of such intertextual references or stylistic kinship can be considered an indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Négritude philosophy in visual arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual artists inspired by Négritude created works based on the same themes; artists trained in Western schools applied Négritude philosophy to promote African culture within modern art contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For visual works, expect motifs that reclaim African aesthetics, portrayals emphasizing black subjectivity, and efforts to integrate African traditions into modernist forms (e.g., Dakar School). Evaluation should consider both form and ideological content—how art resists colonial aesthetics and promotes African cultural value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifesto-like thematic scope (anthology/poetry curation criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthologies and manifestos (e.g., Senghor's and Damas' anthologies) serve as programmatic statements: defining themes, selecting poets, and articulating cultural/political aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling collections or evaluating anthologies, criteria include thematic coherence (anti-colonialism, black consciousness), inclusion of diverse colonial contexts (West Africa, Caribbean, Indochina as Damas suggested), and political clarity. The presence of a preface/manifesto (e.g., Sartre's 'Orphée Noir') that situates the collection historically/philosophically is notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with critiques and debate (self-reflexivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Négritude was subject to criticism (e.g., Achebe, Soyinka) for being too centered on proclaimed ethnic pride; there have been later renaissances and philosophical reappraisals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong contemporary or scholarly works engage with criticisms and show reflexivity—addressing charges of essentialism, eurocentric aesthetic dependence, or insufficiency of militancy. Evaluations should reward acknowledgment of internal debates and developmental complexity.
